tele-001.question: In the TRUST trial (Varma, Circulation 2010), automatic daily remote monitoring of ICDs (Biotronik Home Monitoring) mainly showed:
options: Fewer visits and event detection within 1–2 days, with safety maintained
A significant reduction in all-cause mortality at one year through early detection
A reduction in appropriate shocks thanks to prompt reprogramming
Longer lead longevity thanks to less frequent threshold measurements
commentaires: Correct: about 45% fewer in-hospital evaluations, events identified within 1–2 days versus more than a month, with no excess morbidity.
Incorrect: TRUST was not designed to show a mortality benefit.
Incorrect: appropriate shocks depend on the arrhythmia; remote monitoring does not reduce them per se.
Incorrect: remote monitoring detects lead malfunction earlier but does not extend lead lifespan.
tele-001.explication: TRUST randomised 1339 ICD recipients to automatic daily remote monitoring or conventional in-office follow-up. Remote monitoring reduced in-hospital evaluations by about 45% without increasing morbidity (safety endpoint), and events (AF, VT/VF, lead or generator problems) were identified after a median of 1–2 days versus more than a month with conventional follow-up. The trial was not designed to show a mortality benefit. Remote monitoring does not by itself change the number of appropriate shocks (which depends on the arrhythmia) or lead longevity, but it allows earlier detection of lead malfunction.
tele-001.aRetenir: TRUST: fewer visits, events detected within 1–2 days instead of more than a month, safety maintained.

tele-002.question: The French ECOST trial (Guédon-Moreau, Eur Heart J 2013) on remote monitoring of ICDs notably showed:
options: More appropriate shocks delivered, thanks to better VT detection
Non-inferior safety and roughly half as many inappropriate shocks
Superiority for cardiovascular mortality at two years of follow-up
A reduction in hospitalisations for acute decompensated heart failure
commentaires: Incorrect: remote monitoring does not change the occurrence of treated arrhythmias; its main effect is to reduce avoidable therapies.
Correct: non-inferior safety, about 52% fewer patients receiving inappropriate shocks and far fewer capacitor charges.
Incorrect: ECOST was not designed for mortality.
Incorrect: HF hospitalisations were not an ECOST endpoint.
tele-002.explication: ECOST randomised 433 ICD recipients in France to daily remote monitoring (Home Monitoring) or in-office follow-up. The primary safety endpoint (major adverse events) was non-inferior. Remote monitoring reduced the number of patients receiving inappropriate shocks by about 52% and markedly reduced capacitor charges, with a favourable effect on battery longevity. The reason is simple: lead noise, rapid AF or oversensing are picked up before they trigger therapy. ECOST was not designed to assess mortality or HF hospitalisations.
tele-002.aRetenir: ECOST: remote monitoring is safe and reduces inappropriate shocks and capacitor charges.

tele-003.question: Regarding the IN-TIME trial (Hindricks, Lancet 2014), which statement is correct?
options: It relied on scheduled quarterly transmissions, with no alerts
It showed more hospitalisations, driven by false alerts
It improved a composite clinical score, with lower mortality
It enrolled single-chamber pacemaker patients without heart failure
commentaires: Incorrect: IN-TIME relied on automatic daily multiparameter transmission.
Incorrect: no excess of alert-related hospitalisations was reported.
Correct: fewer patients with a worsened Packer score (18.9% vs 27.2%) and lower all-cause mortality in the remote monitoring arm.
Incorrect: patients had heart failure (NYHA II–III, LVEF ≤35%) and a dual-chamber ICD or CRT-D.
tele-003.explication: IN-TIME enrolled 664 heart failure patients (NYHA II–III, LVEF ≤35%) with a dual-chamber ICD or CRT-D, using automatic daily multiparameter remote monitoring (atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, % BiV pacing, PVCs, activity, etc.). The proportion of patients whose composite score worsened was lower in the remote monitoring arm (18.9% vs 27.2%), and all-cause mortality was also lower. The key is the combination of automatic daily transmission with an organised response (structured telephone contact). Scheduled quarterly transmissions are not the IN-TIME model. The pitfall: this benefit has not been reproduced in every trial, hence the importance of the organisation that responds to alerts.
tele-003.aRetenir: IN-TIME: daily multiparameter remote monitoring + structured response = less clinical worsening in device patients with HF.

tele-004.question: The EVOLVO trial (Landolina, Circulation 2012), which used CareLink with OptiVol alerts in HF patients with an ICD/CRT-D, showed:
options: Fewer urgent contacts (emergency or unscheduled visits) for HF or arrhythmia
More unscheduled visits, triggered by false OptiVol alerts
A halving of all-cause mortality at 16 months of follow-up
No effect on urgent contacts, as the device's audible alarm is just as effective
commentaires: Correct: this was the primary endpoint, reduced by about 35%, with a shorter time to clinical decision.
Incorrect: urgent or unscheduled visits actually fell by about 35%.
Incorrect: with 200 patients, EVOLVO was not powered for mortality.
Incorrect: remotely transmitted alerts proved more effective than the audible alarm, which patients often fail to hear.
tele-004.explication: EVOLVO randomised 200 HF device patients to remote monitoring with alerts (including the OptiVol fluid index) or standard follow-up with office visits and the device audible alarm. The primary endpoint, the number of emergency department or unscheduled visits for HF, arrhythmia or ICD-related events, was reduced by about 35%. The time from event to clinical decision was also shortened. The trial was not powered for mortality. It shows that an automatically transmitted alert is more effective than the audible alarm, which patients often fail to hear.
tele-004.aRetenir: EVOLVO: remote alerts reduce urgent healthcare use and shorten the time to clinical decision.

tele-005.question: True or false: in a pacemaker or ICD patient on remote monitoring, in-person follow-up can be dropped altogether and no further clinic visits are needed.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: in-person visits are spaced out, not abolished (wound check, examination, education, planning of generator replacement).
Correct: remote monitoring is combined with at least one in-person evaluation, typically once a year; only the implantable loop recorder can do without it.
tele-005.explication: The 2015 HRS consensus recommends combining remote monitoring with at least one annual in-person evaluation, rather than calendar-based in-person follow-up alone. The 2023 consensus on the practical management of the remote monitoring clinic goes further: with a continuous and reliable connection, alert-driven follow-up allows scheduled visits to be spaced out even more, but it does not abolish them. The post-implant wound check, clinical examination, some measurements, patient education and planning of generator replacement remain in person, and any loss of connectivity, recent alert or comorbidity calls for more frequent visits. Some situations also require an in-person check (reprogramming, suspected malfunction). The pitfall is to believe that remote monitoring "replaces" the cardiologist; only the implantable loop recorder, a purely diagnostic device, may no longer need routine clinic visits after the wound check.
tele-005.aRetenir: Remote monitoring spaces out in-person visits (typically at least one a year) but does not abolish them.

tele-006.question: The French COMPAS trial (Mabo, Eur Heart J 2012) studied:
options: Pacemaker patients: non-inferiority, with far fewer clinic visits
Loop recorder patients with syncope: faster diagnosis
Smartwatch-detected AF: fewer strokes on a direct oral anticoagulant
CRT-D patients with severe HF: fewer HF hospitalisations
commentaires: Correct: 538 pacemaker patients, non-inferior safety and about 56% fewer outpatient visits.
Incorrect: COMPAS did not study implantable loop recorders.
Incorrect: COMPAS dealt neither with smartwatches nor with anticoagulation.
Incorrect: this is closer to the IN-TIME population; COMPAS involved pacemaker patients.
tele-006.explication: COMPAS randomised 538 pacemaker patients to remote monitoring (Home Monitoring) or in-office follow-up. The safety endpoint (major adverse events) was non-inferior and outpatient visits were reduced by about 56%. Hospitalisations for atrial arrhythmia (6 vs 18) and for stroke (2 vs 8) were less frequent in the remote monitoring arm, thanks to earlier detection of arrhythmias. It is one of the main pieces of evidence supporting remote monitoring of pacemakers, and not only of ICDs.
tele-006.aRetenir: COMPAS: remote monitoring is safe in pacemaker patients and substantially reduces clinic visits.

tele-007.question: Which of the following benefits have been demonstrated by randomised trials of remote monitoring of cardiac implantable electronic devices?
options: Earlier detection of arrhythmic and technical events
Fewer inappropriate shocks in ICD patients
Fewer in-person visits with no loss of safety
Complete elimination of the risk of sudden cardiac death
Reduced all-cause mortality found in every trial
commentaires: Correct: TRUST showed detection within 1–2 days instead of more than a month.
Correct: ECOST roughly halved inappropriate shocks.
Correct: TRUST and COMPAS reduced visits with no loss of safety.
Incorrect: it is the ICD that treats the arrhythmia; remote monitoring only monitors and anticipates.
Incorrect: the mortality benefit remains debated; IN-TIME was positive, other trials neutral.
tele-007.explication: TRUST showed event detection within 1–2 days instead of more than a month, and fewer visits. COMPAS confirmed fewer visits in pacemaker patients. ECOST showed fewer inappropriate shocks and fewer capacitor charges, which preserves the battery. On the other hand, remote monitoring obviously does not "eliminate" the risk of sudden cardiac death: the ICD treats the arrhythmia, while remote monitoring only serves to monitor and anticipate. The mortality benefit remains debated and depends on the organisation that responds to alerts (IN-TIME positive, other trials neutral). The 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines acknowledge that device-based monitoring detects malfunction and arrhythmias, but consider its clinical benefit for HF management (impedance, multiparameter algorithms) poorly demonstrated and make no recommendation, unlike pulmonary artery pressure monitoring (class IIa).
tele-007.aRetenir: Established benefits: early detection, fewer visits, fewer inappropriate shocks, preserved battery.

tele-008.question: True or false: patients on remote monitoring must be told that remote monitoring is not an emergency service and that, if they have serious symptoms, they must call the emergency services (15 in France).
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: transmissions are reviewed during working hours; with serious symptoms, the patient calls the emergency services (15 in France).
Incorrect: no clinic reviews transmissions 24/7; suggesting otherwise leaves the patient waiting for a call-back that will not come in time.
tele-008.explication: Transmissions are reviewed during working hours: the 2023 HRS consensus asks for alerts to be handled within the working day, prioritising critical alerts, but no clinic provides 24/7 review. The 2023 HRS consensus emphasises patient education at enrolment: what remote monitoring does, what it does not do, and what to do in case of symptoms (presyncope, syncope, repeated shocks, chest pain). In France, life-threatening emergencies are handled by the SAMU (15). The classic pitfall: a patient who receives several shocks and "waits for the clinic to call".
tele-008.aRetenir: Remote monitoring is not real-time surveillance: emergency = call the emergency services (15 in France).

tele-009.question: According to the 2023 HRS/EHRA/APHRS/LAHRS consensus, when should a patient ideally be enrolled in remote monitoring after implantation of a cardiac device?
options: At the first in-person check, 3 months after implantation
As early as possible, ideally before hospital discharge
Only if an arrhythmia is detected at the first check
After one year, once lead stability has been established
commentaires: Incorrect: the first weeks are the high-risk period (lead dislodgement, threshold rise); waiting 3 months forfeits this monitoring.
Correct: enrolment and pairing before discharge, at the latest within 2 weeks (2023 HRS consensus).
Incorrect: remote monitoring is not conditional on an event; its very purpose is to detect one.
Incorrect: a patient not connected at the outset is often connected much later, or never.
tele-009.explication: The consensus recommends enrolling the patient and pairing the transmitter as early as possible, ideally before discharge and at the latest within 2 weeks of implantation; for an implantable loop recorder, enrolment before discharge is mandatory. The first weeks are precisely the period at risk of lead dislodgement, threshold rise or complications, and a patient not connected at the outset is often connected much later, or never. Waiting for the first check or for an event defeats the purpose of early monitoring. Early enrolment also makes it possible to confirm that the connection works from the start.
tele-009.aRetenir: Enrol and pair for remote monitoring before hospital discharge.

tele-010.question: In a remote monitoring clinic, what is the expected role of the remote monitoring nurse working under a written protocol?
options: Triage alerts according to the protocol and escalate to the physician
Remotely reprogram the ICD therapy zones according to the protocol
Independently start an anticoagulant for AF confirmed on the EGM
Close alerts judged benign without any physician review
commentaires: Correct: first-line triage, patient contact, documentation and escalation to the physician according to the written protocol.
Incorrect: reprogramming is the physician's responsibility, and remote programming of zones is not a routine function.
Incorrect: the treatment decision (anticoagulation) rests with the physician.
Incorrect: the protocol defines the sign-off pathways; the nurse does not close alerts alone outside this framework.
tele-010.explication: The remote monitoring nurse (or technician/physiologist) provides first-line review: reading transmissions, triaging alerts according to defined criteria and urgency levels, contacting the patient, checking connectivity and documentation. Situations specified in the protocol are passed to the physician, who retains the treatment decision (anticoagulation, antiarrhythmic drugs, reprogramming). In France, tasks delegated beyond the nurse's legal scope of practice are only possible within a formal cooperation protocol (protocole de coopération). Moreover, remote programming of ICD zones is not a routine feature of current remote monitoring systems.
tele-010.aRetenir: Nurse = first-line triage and escalation according to protocol; treatment decision = physician.

tele-011.question: Which elements should be included in a remote monitoring clinic's written alert management protocol?
options: Urgency levels, each with an associated response time
Review of every transmission by the physician before the nurse
Documentation of actions in the patient record
What to do when transmissions stop arriving
Discontinuation of the annual in-person visit
commentaires: Correct: each alert type must have a priority level and a response time.
Incorrect: first-line triage is precisely delegated to the trained nurse or technician, with escalation to the physician.
Correct: every action must be documented, which also has medico-legal implications.
Correct: a disconnected patient is no longer monitored; the protocol must state who calls and within what time frame.
Incorrect: this has no place in an alert protocol and runs counter to the guidelines.
tele-011.explication: The 2023 HRS consensus recommends written protocols defining who does what, within what time frame and how it is documented: urgency level of each alert type, response times, escalation pathway (nurse to physician, physician to patient or emergency services), how the patient is contacted, and documentation. First-line triage is performed by trained non-physician staff: having the physician review every transmission first would invert the workflow and overwhelm the team. Loss of connectivity must also be managed, because a disconnected patient is no longer monitored. Discontinuing the annual visit is not part of an alert protocol and runs counter to the guidelines.
tele-011.aRetenir: An alert protocol = urgency levels + response times + escalation + documentation + management of lost connectivity.

tele-012.question: Describe briefly the typical organisation of a remote monitoring clinic for cardiac implantable electronic devices, from transmitted signal to clinical decision.
tele-012.reponseAttendue: Enrolment and pairing before discharge, with patient education (it is not an emergency service). Receipt of transmissions and alerts on the manufacturer's platform. First-line triage by a trained nurse or technician according to a written protocol (urgency levels, response times). Escalation to the physician (electrophysiologist) for the alerts specified. Patient contact and decision (no action, clinic visit, treatment adjustment, reprogramming, emergency department). Documentation in the patient record. Management of lost connectivity. In-person visits maintained, spaced out according to the protocol (typically at least once a year).
tele-012.explication: The 2023 HRS consensus describes a team-based model with defined roles: trained non-physician staff for first-line review, physicians responsible for decisions, and written protocols so that every alert has a priority level and a response time. The patient's connectivity must be actively monitored, because an unplugged transmitter makes monitoring illusory. Every action must be documented, which also has medico-legal implications. Patient education underpins safety: patients must know when to call the emergency services (15 in France). The pitfall is to organise the receipt of alerts without organising the response.
tele-012.aRetenir: Effective remote monitoring = early connection + protocol-based triage + physician escalation + documentation.

tele-013.question: What key messages do you give a patient when enrolling them in remote monitoring?
tele-013.reponseAttendue: How it works: automatic transmissions, transmitter plugged in near the bed or app running, Bluetooth switched on. It is not an emergency service: data are reviewed during working hours; in case of presyncope, syncope, multiple shocks or chest pain, call the emergency services (15 in France). What to do after a single, well-tolerated shock (contact the clinic, send a manual transmission). Let the clinic know about travel, a house move, a hospital admission or a change of phone. In-person visits continue (typically at least once a year). Information about the data (secure hosting, GDPR).
tele-013.explication: The 2023 HRS consensus makes patient education a cornerstone of remote monitoring: a patient who understands the system stays connected more often and responds appropriately to symptoms. The most dangerous misunderstanding is to believe in real-time surveillance. Information on data protection is also a GDPR requirement. These messages should be repeated at clinic visits and provided in writing.
tele-013.aRetenir: Educate the patient: stay connected, understand that this is not real-time surveillance, and know when to call the emergency services (15 in France).

tele-014.question: True or false: simply setting up automatic transmissions is enough to obtain the clinical benefit of remote monitoring, even without a defined organisation to handle alerts.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: alerts that nobody reads do not protect the patient; the positive trials combined transmission with an organised team.
Correct: the benefit comes from the organised clinical response (protocols, response times, documentation), not from the technology alone.
tele-014.explication: The positive trials (TRUST, ECOST, IN-TIME, EVOLVO) combined automatic transmissions with a team organised to review them and respond within defined time frames. Alerts that nobody reads do not protect the patient and may expose the clinic to liability. The 2023 HRS consensus specifically emphasises staffing, written protocols, response times and documentation. Technology is only a tool: it is the clinical response that delivers the benefit.
tele-014.aRetenir: The benefit of remote monitoring comes from the organisation that responds to alerts, not from transmission alone.

tele-015.question: In France, remote monitoring data from cardiac implantable electronic devices are personal health data. What requirement applies when they are hosted by a third-party provider?
options: No specific requirement provided the data are encrypted
Mandatory hosting on a server located in the cardiology department
Hosting by an HDS-certified provider, in compliance with the GDPR
Written consent from the GP before each transmission
commentaires: Incorrect: encryption is necessary but does not exempt the host from HDS certification.
Incorrect: the data do not need to be physically hosted in the department.
Correct: article L.1111-8 of the French Public Health Code (HDS certification), plus GDPR obligations.
Incorrect: the GP does not have to authorise each transmission.
tele-015.explication: Article L.1111-8 of the French Public Health Code requires that health data hosted on behalf of third parties be hosted by a provider holding HDS (health data hosting) certification. The GDPR also applies: patient information, defined purpose, data minimisation, security and access rights. Encryption is necessary but does not exempt the host from certification. The data do not need to be physically hosted in the department, and the GP does not authorise each transmission.
tele-015.aRetenir: Remote monitoring data = HDS-certified host + GDPR.

tele-016.question: True or false: in France, after the ETAPES pilot phase, remote medical monitoring (including that of cardiac implantable electronic devices) became part of standard reimbursement in 2023.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: remote medical monitoring entered standard reimbursement on 1 July 2023, after ETAPES.
Incorrect: the 2022 Social Security Financing Act provided for this transition, effective on 1 July 2023 (articles L.162-48 et seq. of the Social Security Code).
tele-016.explication: The ETAPES programme (telemedicine pilots to improve care pathways) provided pilot funding for remote monitoring in several conditions, including patients with cardiac implantable electronic devices. The 2022 Social Security Financing Act provided for its transition to standard reimbursement, effective on 1 July 2023. Remote monitoring is now a permanently reimbursed activity (articles L.162-48 et seq. of the French Social Security Code), combining a remote medical monitoring operator with a digital medical device or technical solution. The detailed arrangements (flat-rate payments, registration) are set out in implementing regulations.
tele-016.aRetenir: ETAPES (pilot phase), then standard reimbursement of remote monitoring from 1 July 2023.

tele-017.question: What was the ETAPES programme in France?
options: A pilot funding framework for remote monitoring
A randomised trial comparing two remote monitoring platforms
A French Society of Cardiology guideline on ICD programming
A national registry of defective defibrillation leads
commentaires: Correct: ETAPES provided pilot payment for remote monitoring, including of cardiac devices, before standard reimbursement in 2023.
Incorrect: it was not a randomised trial.
Incorrect: it was not a programming guideline.
Incorrect: ETAPES was not a device registry.
tele-017.explication: ETAPES (telemedicine pilots to improve care pathways) provided pilot payment for remote monitoring of patients with certain chronic conditions, including heart failure and cardiac implantable electronic devices. It was based on specifications defining the remote monitoring operator, the solution provider and therapeutic support. It was neither a registry, nor a randomised trial, nor a programming guideline. It was superseded when remote monitoring entered standard reimbursement in 2023.
tele-017.aRetenir: ETAPES = pilot funding phase for remote monitoring, before standard reimbursement.

tele-018.question: What is the name of Biotronik's remote monitoring system, used in the TRUST, ECOST, COMPAS and IN-TIME trials?
options: CareLink
LATITUDE
Home Monitoring
SmartView
commentaires: Incorrect: CareLink is the Medtronic platform.
Incorrect: LATITUDE is the Boston Scientific platform.
Correct: Biotronik Home Monitoring, with automatic daily transmission via the CardioMessenger.
Incorrect: SmartView is the MicroPort platform.
tele-018.explication: Biotronik Home Monitoring relies on automatic daily transmission of device data to a transmitter (CardioMessenger) and then to the manufacturer's server. This is the technology evaluated in TRUST, ECOST, COMPAS and IN-TIME. CareLink is the Medtronic platform, LATITUDE the Boston Scientific one and SmartView the MicroPort one. Knowing the platforms helps in interpreting the trials: results obtained with daily transmission do not necessarily apply to less frequent transmissions.

tele-019.question: Which of the following manufacturer / remote monitoring platform pairings are correct?
options: Boston Scientific / LATITUDE
Abbott / Merlin.net
Medtronic / SmartView
Biotronik / Home Monitoring
MicroPort / CareLink
commentaires: Correct: LATITUDE is the Boston Scientific platform.
Correct: Merlin.net is the Abbott platform.
Incorrect: SmartView belongs to MicroPort; Medtronic uses CareLink.
Correct: Home Monitoring is the Biotronik platform.
Incorrect: CareLink belongs to Medtronic; MicroPort uses SmartView.
tele-019.explication: Each manufacturer has its own platform: Medtronic CareLink, Abbott Merlin.net, Boston Scientific LATITUDE, Biotronik Home Monitoring and MicroPort SmartView. SmartView therefore belongs to MicroPort and CareLink to Medtronic, hence the two incorrect pairings. In a multi-vendor clinic, the nurse has to consult several platforms with different alert nomenclatures, which the 2023 HRS consensus identifies as an organisational challenge warranting specific training and, where possible, aggregation software. The device manufacturer is shown on the patient's device ID card.
tele-019.aRetenir: CareLink = Medtronic, Merlin.net = Abbott, LATITUDE = Boston Scientific, Home Monitoring = Biotronik, SmartView = MicroPort.

tele-020.question: On which platform are transmissions from Abbott devices reviewed?
options: Merlin.net
LATITUDE
Home Monitoring
CareLink
commentaires: Correct: Abbott uses Merlin.net (Patient Care Network).
Incorrect: LATITUDE is the Boston Scientific platform.
Incorrect: Home Monitoring is the Biotronik platform.
Incorrect: CareLink is the Medtronic platform.
tele-020.explication: Abbott uses Merlin.net (Patient Care Network), which receives transmissions from Abbott pacemakers, ICDs, CRT devices and implantable loop recorders, via a bedside transmitter or, for connected models, a smartphone app. LATITUDE is Boston Scientific, SmartView is MicroPort and CareLink is Medtronic. In practice, the nurse needs to know which platform to open according to the device manufacturer, which is shown on the device ID card.

tele-021.question: A patient with a MicroPort CRM pacemaker (formerly Sorin/LivaNova) needs to be enrolled in remote monitoring. Which platform is used?
options: LATITUDE
SmartView
Home Monitoring
Merlin.net
commentaires: Incorrect: LATITUDE is the Boston Scientific platform.
Correct: MicroPort CRM devices, successors to the Sorin range, are remotely monitored via SmartView.
Incorrect: Home Monitoring is the Biotronik platform.
Incorrect: Merlin.net is the Abbott platform.
tele-021.explication: MicroPort CRM devices, successors to the Sorin range, are remotely monitored via the SmartView platform, with a home transmitter. Home Monitoring is Biotronik, Merlin.net is Abbott and LATITUDE is Boston Scientific. The 2023 HRS consensus stresses that clinics must manage several platforms with different features and alert nomenclatures, which warrants specific staff training.

tele-022.question: On CareLink, a patient with a Medtronic CRT-D has an "OptiVol" alert. What does this index measure?
options: A fall in intrathoracic impedance, reflecting congestion
The night-time respiratory rate, measured by the accelerometer
The percentage of biventricular pacing over recent days
Pulmonary artery pressure, estimated by a lead sensor
commentaires: Correct: the index accumulates the fall in impedance measured between the RV lead and the can relative to a reference.
Incorrect: respiratory rate is a separate parameter, not included in the OptiVol index.
Incorrect: % BiV pacing is a separate counter, unrelated to the fluid index.
Incorrect: pulmonary pressure requires dedicated implantable sensors, not OptiVol.
tele-022.explication: OptiVol is based on repeated measurement of intrathoracic impedance between the right ventricular lead and the can. When fluid accumulates in the chest, impedance falls; the fluid index accumulates the difference between daily impedance and a reference value and triggers an alert above a programmable threshold. Yu et al. showed that the fall in impedance preceded HF hospitalisation by several days. It does not measure pulmonary pressure (dedicated implantable sensors), respiratory rate or % BiV pacing, which are separate parameters.
tele-022.aRetenir: OptiVol = fall in intrathoracic impedance, an indirect sign of congestion.

tele-023.question: The HeartLogic algorithm (Boston Scientific) combines several sensors to compute a decompensation risk index. Which of the following is NOT part of it?
options: Heart sounds (S1, S3)
Thoracic impedance
Respiratory rate
NT-proBNP level
commentaires: Incorrect: S1 and S3 are measured by the accelerometer and are part of the index.
Incorrect: thoracic impedance is one of the HeartLogic sensors.
Incorrect: respiratory rate and the rate/tidal volume ratio are part of the index.
Correct: the device does not measure NT-proBNP, although this test helps to interpret an alert.
tele-023.explication: HeartLogic, validated in the MultiSENSE study, integrates device-derived data only: S1 and S3 heart sounds (accelerometer), thoracic impedance, respiratory rate and the respiratory rate/tidal volume ratio, night-time heart rate and activity. The device obviously does not measure NT-proBNP, although this test is very useful for interpreting an alert. The pitfall is to think that the algorithm relies on a single sensor: it is precisely the combination that improves sensitivity compared with impedance alone.
tele-023.aRetenir: HeartLogic = S1/S3 + impedance + respiration + night-time heart rate + activity, with no laboratory data.

tele-024.question: True or false: in the MultiSENSE study, the HeartLogic index alert threshold was set at 16.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: an index above 16 defined entry into the alert state in MultiSENSE; it is also the nominal value.
Incorrect: 16 is indeed the validated entry threshold; the default recovery threshold is 6.
tele-024.explication: In MultiSENSE, a HeartLogic index crossing the threshold of 16 defined entry into the alert state; this is also the nominal value used in practice, which can then be reprogrammed. The alert state ends when the index falls below the recovery threshold (6 by default). With this threshold, sensitivity for HF events was about 70%, with a median warning time of about one month and an unexplained alert rate of about 1.5 per patient-year. The threshold is not a "diagnosis": the alert must be interpreted alongside the clinical picture (weight, breathlessness, oedema), other device data and, where appropriate, laboratory tests.
tele-024.aRetenir: HeartLogic: alert above an index of 16 (the value validated in MultiSENSE).

tele-025.question: How did the HeartLogic algorithm perform in the MultiSENSE study (nominal threshold)?
options: Sensitivity about 50%, median warning time about 3 months
Sensitivity about 70%, median warning time about 34 days
Sensitivity about 70%, median warning time about 48 hours
Sensitivity about 90%, median warning time about 7 days
commentaires: Incorrect: sensitivity was higher (about 70%) and the median warning time about one month.
Correct: about 70% of HF events detected, a median warning time of 34 days, about 1.5 unexplained alerts per patient-year.
Incorrect: the sensitivity is right, but the warning time was about one month; this long lead time is what makes it clinically useful.
Incorrect: no algorithm reaches such a sensitivity, and the warning time was much longer.
tele-025.explication: In MultiSENSE, HeartLogic detected about 70% of HF events, with a median warning time of 34 days and an unexplained alert rate of about 1.47 per patient-year, much better than thoracic impedance alone. No algorithm approaches 100% sensitivity or perfect specificity. The long lead time, about a month rather than a few hours, is what makes it clinically useful: it leaves time to adjust diuretics and treatment before decompensation. The pitfall is to place too much trust in the absence of an alert: 30% of events are not preceded by one.
tele-025.aRetenir: HeartLogic: ~70% sensitivity, ~1 month warning time, ~1.5 unexplained alerts per patient-year.

tele-026.question: Alert transmission from a 70-year-old patient with a Medtronic CRT-D: the OptiVol fluid index crossed the threshold 5 days ago. No arrhythmia, 99% BiV pacing. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Close the alert and recheck the index at the next scheduled transmission, as OptiVol has low specificity
Call the patient the same day (weight, breathlessness, oedema, adherence, salt), then decide on clinical grounds
Send the patient to the emergency department the same day for a decompensation work-up and intravenous diuretics
Increase the diuretic straight away by letter to the GP, then recheck the index in one month
commentaires: Incorrect (under-reaction): low specificity means the alert must be checked against the clinical picture, not ignored; this forfeits the benefit shown in EVOLVO.
Correct: a prompt but non-life-threatening alert; call within the working day, look for congestion and triggers, then adjust treatment or arrange a visit.
Incorrect (over-reaction): without red flags, an isolated OptiVol alert does not warrant immediate admission.
Incorrect: blindly treating a non-specific index without speaking to the patient risks dehydration and misses an alternative cause.
tele-026.explication: An isolated OptiVol alert, with no arrhythmia or loss of resynchronisation, calls for prompt but non-emergency management: an early telephone call (the 2023 HRS consensus asks for every alert to be handled within the working day) and a search for signs of congestion and triggers (dietary indiscretion, stopping medication, NSAIDs, infection). Depending on the findings, diuretics are adjusted, a clinic visit is arranged, or blood tests (NT-proBNP, renal function) are requested. Immediate admission is not justified without red flags. Conversely, closing the alert without a call forfeits the benefit demonstrated in EVOLVO: low specificity means the alert must be checked against the clinical picture, not ignored. Blindly increasing diuretics without questioning the patient is the other pitfall: the index can rise for another reason (chest infection, effusion).
tele-026.aRetenir: OptiVol alert = call the patient and check against the clinical picture; neither panic nor closing it without action.

tele-027.question: True or false: an isolated rise in the OptiVol fluid index is enough to establish heart failure decompensation.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: impedance is sensitive but not very specific (infection, effusion, pocket haematoma, posture).
Correct: the alert must be checked against the clinical picture and other parameters; it is not a diagnosis.
tele-027.explication: A fall in intrathoracic impedance is sensitive but not very specific: a chest infection, a pleural effusion, a recent device pocket or a haematoma, or even changes in posture can alter it. This is why the alert must be checked against the clinical picture and other parameters (night-time heart rate, activity, AF burden, % BiV). Multiparameter algorithms (TriageHF, HeartLogic) were developed to improve this specificity. The pitfall: prescribing diuretics blindly on the basis of an isolated index.
tele-027.aRetenir: Isolated OptiVol = a warning sign to be verified, not a diagnosis.

tele-028.question: The TriageHF risk status (Medtronic) classifies the patient as low, medium or high risk. What does a "high risk" status mean?
options: An increased risk of an HF event within 30 days, warranting a call
An ongoing ventricular arrhythmia, warranting an emergency call
An indication for upgrade to CRT-D, to be discussed in clinic
A battery close to ERI, warranting planned replacement
commentaires: Correct: it estimates the risk of HF hospitalisation within 30 days and warrants a structured call and clinical assessment.
Incorrect: this status estimates a short-term risk; it does not signal an acute arrhythmia.
Incorrect: it is not an indication for a device.
Incorrect: TriageHF provides no information on battery status.
tele-028.explication: TriageHF integrates several device diagnostics (OptiVol fluid index, AT/AF burden and ventricular rate during AF, activity, night-time heart rate, heart rate variability, % pacing, ventricular arrhythmias, shocks) to estimate the risk of HF hospitalisation over the next 30 days. In the prospective TRIAGE-HF study (100 patients), each "high" status triggered a structured call: it corresponded to signs or symptoms of worsening HF in 63% of cases, and in 83% when non-adherence (medication, diet) was included. The parameters most often involved were the OptiVol index, reduced activity and a raised night-time heart rate. This status signals neither end of battery life nor an acute arrhythmia, and is not an indication for a device. Same logic as PARTNERS-HF: it is the combination of parameters that matters.
tele-028.aRetenir: TriageHF "high" = increased short-term risk of an HF event: call and assess.

tele-029.question: Which of the following parameters are routinely provided by implanted devices and useful for detecting worsening heart failure?
options: Thoracic impedance
Night-time heart rate
Daily weight measured by the device
Arterial oxygen saturation
AF burden and ventricular rate during AF
commentaires: Correct: a fall reflects intrathoracic fluid accumulation.
Correct: it rises with decompensation.
Incorrect: the device does not weigh the patient; weight comes from scales, which may be connected.
Incorrect: cardiac implantable devices do not measure oxygen saturation.
Correct: AF is both a cause and a consequence of decompensation.
tele-029.explication: Modern ICDs and CRT devices measure thoracic impedance, night-time heart rate (which rises with decompensation), activity (which falls) and AF burden with the associated ventricular rate (AF is both a cause and a consequence of decompensation). Heart rate variability and % BiV pacing complete these data. Neither weight nor oxygen saturation is measured by cardiac implantable devices: weight comes from scales, sometimes connected to an HF remote monitoring platform. No single parameter is sufficient: it is their combination that carries prognostic value, as in PARTNERS-HF.
tele-029.aRetenir: Impedance, night-time heart rate, activity, AF, % BiV: a body of device-derived evidence, never a single parameter.

tele-031.question: CRT-D: BiV pacing has fallen from 99% to 86% in one month. AF burden is 45%, with a mean ventricular rate during AF of 105 bpm. No significant PVCs. What is the most likely cause and the approach?
options: ERI: the device restricts BiV pacing, plan generator replacement
Atrial oversensing: reduce atrial sensitivity at the next scheduled check
Loss of LV capture: urgently reprogram LV amplitude or vector
Rapidly conducted AF: call, check anticoagulation, control the rate
commentaires: Incorrect: the battery has nothing to do with this picture.
Incorrect: AF is documented by the burden and ventricular rate; nothing suggests oversensing.
Incorrect: loss of LV capture does not lower the counter, because the device keeps pacing.
Correct: intrinsically conducted QRS complexes inhibit BiV pacing; rate control, or even AV node ablation, and check anticoagulation.
tele-031.explication: When AF is conducted rapidly, intrinsic QRS complexes inhibit BiV pacing and the percentage falls: this is the most common cause of loss of resynchronisation. Anticoagulation (CHA2DS2-VA), tolerance and precipitating factors must be checked, and then either the rate controlled (beta-blocker, digoxin), sinus rhythm restored, or AV node ablation considered, which guarantees BiV pacing close to 100% (an option provided for by the 2021 ESC guidelines in CRT patients with AF whose BiV pacing remains insufficient). Loss of LV capture does not lower the BiV pacing counter, because the device keeps pacing. The battery has nothing to do with it.
tele-031.aRetenir: Falling % BiV + rapid AF: control the rate, or even ablate the AV node, and check anticoagulation.

tele-032.question: Which situations can lower the percentage of biventricular pacing displayed by a CRT device?
options: AF with rapid AV conduction
Frequent PVCs
Intrinsic AV conduction that has become shorter than the programmed AV delay
Loss of LV capture due to a threshold rise
Shortening of the programmed AV delay
commentaires: Correct: intrinsically conducted QRS complexes inhibit BiV pacing.
Correct: each PVC is a non-resynchronised beat.
Correct: the native QRS occurs before the end of the AV delay and inhibits pacing.
Incorrect: the device keeps pacing, so the counter stays at 99% even though the patient is no longer resynchronised.
Incorrect: shortening the AV delay actually increases pacing.
tele-032.explication: The BiV pacing counter records cycles in which the device paces, not those in which it captures. Rapid AF, PVCs and intrinsic AV conduction faster than the programmed AV delay (for example on sympathomimetic drugs or during exercise) produce intrinsic QRS complexes and lower the percentage. Loss of LV capture is the classic pitfall: the device keeps delivering its pulses and the counter stays at 99%, even though the patient is no longer resynchronised. It must be sought on the ECG and by measuring the LV threshold. Shortening the AV delay actually increases pacing.
tele-032.aRetenir: A normal % BiV does not rule out loss of LV capture: the counter counts paced beats, not captured beats.

tele-033.question: CRT patient with clinical deterioration. Remote monitoring: BiV pacing 99%, no AF, no PVCs, stable impedances, stable RV threshold. The automatically measured LV threshold has risen from 1.0 V to 3.0 V (at 0.4 ms), with the LV output programmed at 2.5 V. What is the most likely interpretation?
options: Normal situation: a 99% counter guarantees effective resynchronisation
Loss of LV capture masked by the counter: check and reprogram
T-wave oversensing on the LV lead: adjust LV sensitivity
Battery depletion: the measured threshold rises, plan replacement
commentaires: Incorrect: the counter counts delivered pulses, not captured beats; here it is misleading.
Correct: LV threshold (3.0 V) > output (2.5 V): only RV pacing is effective; ECG, threshold test, amplitude or vector, look for dislodgement.
Incorrect: oversensing does not produce this picture and does not explain an LV threshold of 3 V.
Incorrect: battery depletion does not raise the LV capture threshold.
tele-033.explication: With an LV threshold of 3.0 V and an output of 2.5 V, LV pacing no longer captures: the patient is paced from the RV only, which can worsen dyssynchrony and HF. The 99% BiV counter is misleading, because it counts delivered pulses. Management is a prompt device check: 12-lead ECG (pure RV-paced QRS morphology), threshold test, increased amplitude or change of vector (quadripolar leads), chest X-ray to look for dislodgement. Automatic LV capture management, where available, only adjusts the output if it is programmed in adaptive mode (rather than measurement only), and within the maximum permitted amplitude. T-wave oversensing or a depleted battery do not produce this picture.
tele-033.aRetenir: LV threshold > programmed amplitude = loss of resynchronisation masked by a normal % BiV.

tele-034.question: CRT-D: BiV pacing is 90%, with 8% PVCs counted by the device. No AF. What is your approach?
tele-034.reponseAttendue: Confirm on the EGMs that these really are PVCs (and not oversensing). Contact the patient (symptoms, HF). Look for precipitating factors: potassium, magnesium, ischaemia, decompensation, medications. Quantify and characterise the PVCs (Holter monitoring, morphology). Optimise treatment (beta-blocker, possibly amiodarone) and consider PVC ablation if they are monomorphic and frequent. PVC-triggered pacing features provide only partial resynchronisation. Target: ≥98% BiV pacing.
tele-034.explication: Frequent PVCs are, together with AF, the main cause of loss of BiV pacing. A burden of 8–10% is enough to reduce the benefit of resynchronisation and can also perpetuate a cardiomyopathy. A counting artefact (T-wave oversensing, double counting) must first be excluded on the EGMs. Correction of triggers and drug optimisation come next, then radiofrequency ablation, which can restore near-complete BiV pacing. Features that trigger LV pacing on RV sensing provide only partial resynchronisation and do not replace treatment of the cause.
tele-034.aRetenir: PVCs above a few % in a CRT patient: treat the cause, with drugs or ablation, to get back to ≥98% BiV.

tele-035.question: Boston Scientific CRT-D: HeartLogic alert (index above threshold for 10 days). On the same transmission: AF that started 12 days ago, mean ventricular rate 110 bpm, BiV pacing down from 98% to 85%. The patient is not anticoagulated. What is your analysis and management?
tele-035.reponseAttendue: Review the EGMs (true AF). Likely sequence: rapid AF → loss of resynchronisation → congestion (HeartLogic). Call the patient promptly (signs of congestion, tolerance) and arrange an early review. Anticoagulation according to CHA2DS2-VA (prolonged AF, often confirmed on ECG). Treat congestion (diuretics). Control the rate or restore rhythm (cardioversion after effective anticoagulation or TOE), and consider AV node ablation if BiV pacing remains insufficient. Monitor the return of the index and % BiV.
tele-035.explication: This case illustrates the value of reading the transmission as a whole rather than alert by alert: rapidly conducted AF causes loss of resynchronisation, which worsens HF, detected by HeartLogic. The priority is clinical (tolerance, congestion), followed by thromboembolic prevention: 12 days of AF is no longer a brief episode and will usually be documented on an ECG. Getting back to ≥98% BiV pacing requires rate or rhythm control, or even AV node ablation, which the 2021 ESC guidelines provide for in CRT patients with AF. Treating congestion alone without correcting the AF would invite recurrence.
tele-035.aRetenir: HF alert + rapid AF + falling % BiV: a single story, to be addressed in order: tolerance, anticoagulation, rate/rhythm, resynchronisation.

tele-036.question: What does the acronym AHRE stand for in a remote monitoring transmission?
options: A bleeding alert on anticoagulation, transmitted by the device
A rapid atrial episode detected by the device, to be confirmed on the EGM
A hypotension alert, calculated from thoracic impedance data
A high-risk ventricular episode, treated or not by the ICD
commentaires: Incorrect: no device detects bleeding.
Correct: atrial high-rate episode, to be validated on the EGM (AF, flutter, atrial tachycardia or artefact).
Incorrect: cardiac devices do not measure blood pressure.
Incorrect: AHRE refers to an atrial episode, not a ventricular one.
tele-036.explication: An AHRE (atrial high-rate episode) is an episode detected by the atrial lead of a pacemaker or ICD above a programmed atrial rate for a minimum duration. It may correspond to AF, atrial flutter or atrial tachycardia, but also to artefacts (far-field R-wave oversensing, noise). This is why reviewing the EGM is essential before any decision. Once confirmed, the episode is classified as subclinical AF, which is distinct from clinical AF documented on an ECG.
tele-036.aRetenir: AHRE = rapid atrial episode detected by the device, to be validated on the EGM before any decision.

tele-037.question: An "AF episode" alert arrives on the platform for a patient with a dual-chamber pacemaker. What is the first step?
options: Send the patient to the emergency department for an ECG and work-up the same day
Program the device to VVI to avoid tracking the AF
Prescribe an anticoagulant by telephone based on CHA2DS2-VA
Review the stored EGMs to confirm a true atrial arrhythmia
commentaires: Incorrect (over-reaction): referring to the emergency department before checking the episode leads to unnecessary decisions.
Incorrect: mode switching already prevents AF tracking; changing mode without a diagnosis makes no sense.
Incorrect: prescribing before checking the EGM risks anticoagulating an artefact (far-field, noise).
Correct: many "AF" episodes are artefacts; reviewing the atrial EGM is the first step.
tele-037.explication: Not every episode classified as "AF" by the device is true AF: far-field R-wave oversensing, noise, interference or repetitive PACs can trigger the counter. Reviewing the atrial EGM (rapid, disorganised activity, dissociated from the ventricle) is the first step. Next come duration and burden, ventricular rate, symptoms, CHA2DS2-VA score and current treatment. Prescribing or referring to the emergency department before this check leads to unnecessary or dangerous decisions.
tele-037.aRetenir: Always review the EGM before concluding that AF is present.

tele-038.question: Calculate the CHA2DS2-VA score (ESC 2024) of a 78-year-old woman with hypertension and a history of TIA, with no other risk factors.
commentaires: Incorrect: 3 points overlooks the fact that age ≥75 years and TIA each score 2 points.
Incorrect: 4 points underestimates the score (one of the 2-point items counted as 1).
Correct: age ≥75 years (2) + hypertension (1) + TIA (2) = 5.
Incorrect: 6 corresponds to CHA2DS2-VASc, which still counts female sex.
tele-038.explication: The ESC 2024 CHA2DS2-VA score removes the "female sex" criterion from CHA2DS2-VASc. Here: age ≥75 years = 2 points, hypertension = 1 point, prior stroke/TIA/thromboembolism = 2 points, giving 5. With CHA2DS2-VASc, the score would have been 6 by adding female sex, hence the distractor. For clinical AF, the 2024 ESC guidelines recommend anticoagulation from 2 points (class I) and state that it should be considered at 1 point (class IIa).
tele-038.aRetenir: CHA2DS2-VA: female sex no longer counts; age ≥75 years and stroke/TIA score 2 points each.

tele-039.question: True or false: in the CHA2DS2-VA score of the 2024 ESC guidelines, female sex scores 1 point.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: the ESC 2024 CHA2DS2-VA score specifically removes the female sex criterion.
Correct: CHA2DS2-VA = CHA2DS2-VASc without female sex; the same thresholds apply to men and women.
tele-039.explication: The 2024 ESC guidelines adopted CHA2DS2-VA, which removes the "female sex" criterion (Sc) from CHA2DS2-VASc. Female sex was mainly a risk modifier in the presence of other factors, and its removal simplifies decision-making: the same thresholds apply to men and women. The other items are unchanged: HF, hypertension, age ≥75 years (2), diabetes, stroke/TIA/thromboembolism (2), vascular disease, age 65–74 years. The pitfall is to use the old score out of habit in remote monitoring reports.

tele-040.question: True or false: according to the 2024 ESC guidelines, "clinical" AF requires documentation on a 12-lead ECG, or on a single- or multiple-lead ECG tracing of at least 30 seconds.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: this is the ESC 2024 definition of clinical AF (12-lead, or ≥30 s on one or more leads).
Incorrect: an episode seen only by the device is subclinical AF; clinical AF requires ECG documentation.
tele-040.explication: The 2024 ESC guidelines define clinical AF by ECG documentation: a 12-lead ECG, or a single- or multiple-lead tracing of at least 30 seconds showing irregular RR intervals without distinct P waves. Episodes detected only by an implanted device (intracardiac EGM) are termed subclinical AF once the EGM has been confirmed. This distinction is crucial: the evidence on anticoagulation differs, because the thromboembolic risk of subclinical AF is lower. An episode detected by the device and then found on an ECG becomes clinical AF.
tele-040.aRetenir: Clinical AF = ECG; subclinical AF = detection by the device alone.

tele-041.question: A 72-year-old man with a DDD pacemaker for AV block, hypertension and diabetes, and no history of stroke. Remote monitoring shows a 4-hour episode confirmed as AF on the EGM, with no AF on ECGs. CHA2DS2-VA = 3. Low bleeding risk. What management is most consistent with the 2024 ESC guidelines?
options: Discuss a DOAC (class IIb) with the patient, keep monitoring
Mandatory DOAC, as for clinical AF (class I), starting today
Long-term aspirin, a good compromise between stroke and bleeding risk
No action: an episode seen only by the device has no significance
commentaires: Correct: subclinical AF of intermediate duration, high risk, low bleeding risk: a DOAC may be considered (IIb); monitor for progression.
Incorrect (over-reaction): this is subclinical AF, for which the 2024 ESC guidelines give only a class IIb recommendation.
Incorrect: aspirin is not a recommended alternative for stroke prevention in AF.
Incorrect (under-reaction): the episode is confirmed and the thromboembolic risk is high; it should at least be discussed.
tele-041.explication: This is subclinical AF of intermediate duration (more than a few minutes, less than 24 h), exactly the population of ARTESiA and NOAH-AFNET 6. In ARTESiA, apixaban reduced stroke and systemic embolism compared with aspirin, at the cost of more major bleeding. In NOAH-AFNET 6, edoxaban did not significantly reduce the primary endpoint and increased bleeding. The 2024 ESC guidelines drew a class IIb recommendation from these trials: a DOAC may be considered in patients at high thromboembolic risk, excluding those at high bleeding risk, after shared decision-making. Aspirin is not a recommended alternative for stroke prevention in AF. Monitoring for progression to longer or clinical AF is essential.
tele-041.aRetenir: Confirmed subclinical AF at high risk: discuss a DOAC (IIb), shared decision-making.

tele-042.question: Regarding the ARTESiA trial (Healey, NEJM 2024), which statement is correct?
options: Apixaban vs aspirin in subclinical AF: fewer strokes and less bleeding
Apixaban vs placebo in clinical AF: fewer strokes, similar bleeding
Apixaban vs aspirin in subclinical AF: no reduction in strokes
Apixaban vs aspirin in subclinical AF: fewer strokes, more bleeding
commentaires: Incorrect: major bleeding was more frequent on apixaban (about 1.7% vs 0.9% per year).
Incorrect: the comparator was aspirin and the AF was subclinical.
Incorrect: stroke and systemic embolism were reduced by about 37%.
Correct: stroke and systemic embolism reduced by about 37%, at the cost of more major bleeding.
tele-042.explication: ARTESiA enrolled about 4000 patients aged 55 years or over with a pacemaker, ICD or implantable monitor, subclinical AF lasting 6 minutes to 24 hours and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of at least 3. Apixaban reduced stroke and systemic embolism by about 37% compared with aspirin (about 0.8% vs 1.2% per year), with a higher rate of major bleeding (about 1.7% vs 0.9% per year). The absolute stroke risk therefore remains low, well below that of clinical AF. The comparator was aspirin, not placebo, and the patients had subclinical AF, not clinical AF.
tele-042.aRetenir: ARTESiA: apixaban > aspirin for stroke in subclinical AF, but more bleeding and a low absolute risk.

tele-043.question: What was the main result of the NOAH-AFNET 6 trial (Kirchhof, NEJM 2023) in patients with atrial high-rate episodes (AHRE)?
options: Edoxaban superior to placebo for stroke, at the cost of more bleeding
Early termination, no significant reduction in events, more bleeding
Stroke rate of about 5% per year on placebo, justifying anticoagulation
Halving of all-cause mortality on edoxaban, with no excess bleeding
commentaires: Incorrect: edoxaban did not significantly reduce the efficacy endpoint.
Correct: stopped for futility and a safety signal; the composite of death or major bleeding was increased.
Incorrect: the stroke rate on placebo was low, about 1% per year.
Incorrect: no mortality benefit, and bleeding was more frequent.
tele-043.explication: NOAH-AFNET 6 randomised about 2500 patients aged 65 years or over, with at least one risk factor and AHREs lasting at least 6 minutes, to edoxaban or placebo. The trial was stopped early for futility and because of a safety signal. Edoxaban did not significantly reduce the efficacy endpoint and increased the composite of death or major bleeding. The stroke rate on placebo was low (about 1% per year), well below that of clinical AF. This result, which contrasts with ARTESiA, explains the cautious recommendation (class IIb) in the 2024 ESC guidelines.
tele-043.aRetenir: NOAH-AFNET 6: no significant benefit of edoxaban for AHREs, more bleeding, strokes rare.

tele-044.question: The meta-analysis of NOAH-AFNET 6 and ARTESiA (McIntyre, Circulation 2024) showed that, in device-detected AF, DOACs:
options: Reduce all-cause mortality by a third, at the cost of more bleeding
Have no effect on ischaemic stroke but increase major bleeding
Reduce ischaemic stroke by a third, more bleeding, mortality unchanged
Reduce ischaemic stroke and, paradoxically, major bleeding
commentaires: Incorrect: the meta-analysis showed no difference in cardiovascular or all-cause mortality.
Incorrect: this is the conclusion one would draw from NOAH-AFNET 6 alone; pooled, the trials show about 32% fewer ischaemic strokes.
Correct: RR for ischaemic stroke around 0.68, major bleeding increased by about 60%, mortality unchanged.
Incorrect: major bleeding increased by about 60%.
tele-044.explication: Pooling the two trials, DOACs reduced ischaemic stroke by about 32% (relative risk around 0.68) and increased major bleeding by about 60%, with no difference in cardiovascular or all-cause mortality. The absolute benefit therefore depends on the patient's baseline thromboembolic and bleeding risks. This meta-analysis informed the class IIb recommendation in the 2024 ESC guidelines. The pitfall is to conclude "no effect" from NOAH-AFNET 6 alone, or "same effect as in clinical AF" from ARTESiA alone.
tele-044.aRetenir: Device-detected AF: DOACs = one third fewer ischaemic strokes, more bleeding, no effect on mortality.

tele-045.question: An 80-year-old woman with hypertension and a pacemaker. Remote monitoring: a continuous 36-hour AF episode, typical EGM, patient asymptomatic, not anticoagulated, bleeding risk not high. What do you propose?
options: No immediate action: asymptomatic subclinical AF, review at the annual check
Long-term aspirin and reassessment after the next transmission
Refer to the emergency department for immediate electrical cardioversion before anticoagulation
Call the patient, obtain an ECG if possible and offer oral anticoagulation
commentaires: Incorrect (under-reaction): an episode lasting more than 24 h is associated with a markedly increased stroke risk (ASSERT).
Incorrect: aspirin is not an alternative to anticoagulation.
Incorrect (over-reaction): asymptomatic patient, AF for more than 24 h: cardioversion without prior anticoagulation carries a risk of embolism.
Correct: episode >24 h, CHA2DS2-VA of 3: in practice it is treated as clinical AF.
tele-045.explication: In the ASSERT analysis by duration, only subclinical AF episodes lasting more than 24 hours were associated with a significant increase in stroke risk. The ARTESiA and NOAH-AFNET 6 trials in fact excluded episodes lasting more than 24 h. In this patient with a CHA2DS2-VA score of 3 (age ≥75 years = 2, hypertension = 1), most experts consider that such a long episode warrants anticoagulation, all the more so if it is confirmed on an ECG, which makes it clinical AF. Aspirin is not an alternative. Emergency cardioversion is not indicated in an asymptomatic patient, and AF lasting more than 24 h is not cardioverted without prior anticoagulation (or TOE).
tele-045.aRetenir: Device-detected AF >24 h in an at-risk patient: in practice it is treated as clinical AF.

tele-046.question: A 58-year-old pacemaker patient with no risk factors (CHA2DS2-VA = 0). Remote monitoring shows a single 40-second AF episode confirmed on the EGM. What is the appropriate management?
options: Immediate oral anticoagulation, since the episode is confirmed on the device EGM
Planned admission for cardioversion and aetiological work-up of AF
No anticoagulation; monitor AF burden, manage risk factors
Long-term aspirin, then review AF burden in one year
commentaires: Incorrect (over-reaction): a brief episode in a patient with no risk factors does not warrant anticoagulation.
Incorrect: cardioversion makes no sense for an asymptomatic 40-second episode that has already ended.
Correct: very low thromboembolic risk; monitor for progression and manage risk factors.
Incorrect: aspirin has no role in stroke prevention in AF.
tele-046.explication: A brief, isolated episode in a patient with no risk factors carries a very low thromboembolic risk: no evidence supports anticoagulation, and aspirin has no role in this setting. The 2024 ESC guidelines emphasise monitoring for progression (longer episodes, clinical AF) and managing risk factors and comorbidities (hypertension, weight, alcohol, sleep apnoea). Remote monitoring is precisely what allows the AF burden to be followed over time. Cardioversion makes no sense for an asymptomatic 40-second episode.
tele-046.aRetenir: Brief episode, CHA2DS2-VA of 0: no anticoagulation, monitor for progression.

tele-047.question: Dual-chamber pacemaker: numerous "AF episodes" with mode switching. On the EGM, the atrial channel senses, on every cycle, an event about 80–120 ms after each QRS, in addition to the sinus P wave. The ventricular rhythm is regular. What is the most likely interpretation?
options: Pacemaker-mediated tachycardia triggered by a PVC
Far-field R-wave oversensing by the atrial lead
Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction, every other F wave hidden
True paroxysmal AF, with anticoagulation to be discussed
commentaires: Incorrect: PMT causes ventricular pacing at the upper rate, not an atrial signal at a fixed coupling interval with a regular rhythm.
Correct: an atrial event at a fixed interval after each QRS is the hallmark of far-field R-wave sensing, which doubles the apparent atrial rate.
Incorrect: flutter would produce regular F waves independent of the QRS.
Incorrect: these false episodes must certainly not lead to anticoagulation.
tele-047.explication: An atrial event sensed at a fixed interval after each QRS, with otherwise regular sinus activity, is the hallmark of far-field sensing of the ventricular signal by the atrial lead. The apparent atrial rate doubles, crosses the atrial tachycardia detection threshold and triggers inappropriate mode switching and false "AF" episodes. The fix is to lengthen the post-ventricular atrial blanking period or reduce atrial sensitivity, without losing detection of true AF. These false episodes must certainly not lead to anticoagulation. 2:1 flutter would produce regular F waves independent of the QRS.
tele-047.aRetenir: Atrial event at a fixed coupling interval after each QRS = far-field R wave, not AF.

tele-048.question: AF alert in a patient with a dual-chamber ICD. Which elements should you analyse?
options: The ventricular rate during AF and how close it comes to the VT/VF zones
Anticoagulation status and CHA2DS2-VA score
Any inappropriate therapies delivered
Whether to disable ICD therapies during AF episodes
Whether to program the device to DDD without mode switching to track the AF
commentaires: Correct: rapid AF close to the detection zones exposes the patient to inappropriate therapy.
Correct: thromboembolic risk is one of the three consequences to assess.
Correct: remote monitoring allows them to be identified, or even anticipated (ECOST).
Incorrect: disabling therapies would leave the patient unprotected; act on the rate and the programming instead.
Incorrect: without mode switching, the ventricle would be paced at the maximum tracking rate.
tele-048.explication: In an ICD patient, AF has three consequences to assess: thromboembolic risk (duration, burden, CHA2DS2-VA, anticoagulation), the risk of inappropriate therapy if the ventricular rate approaches the detection zones, and haemodynamic impact (HF, loss of BiV pacing with CRT). Remote monitoring makes it possible to act before an inappropriate shock, as ECOST showed, by controlling the rate and adjusting the programming (zones, discriminators); disabling therapies would leave the patient unprotected. Turning off mode switching to track AF in DDD would also be a mistake: the ventricle would be paced at the maximum tracking rate.
tele-048.aRetenir: AF in an ICD patient: thromboembolic risk, risk of inappropriate shock and impact on HF.

tele-049.question: A patient already anticoagulated for known paroxysmal AF. Remote monitoring has shown persistent AF (100% burden) for 3 weeks, with a mean ventricular rate of 75 bpm. The patient is asymptomatic. What level of urgency and what management?
options: No action: the patient is anticoagulated and rate-controlled, close the alert
Stop the anticoagulant by telephone, as the AF is now permanent and stable
Urgent: send the patient to the emergency department today for electrical cardioversion
Non-urgent: inform the responsible physician and book a visit (rhythm control)
commentaires: Incorrect (under-reaction): doing nothing misses a window to restore sinus rhythm; this is a marker of progression.
Incorrect: thromboembolic risk does not fall when AF becomes persistent or permanent; stopping would be a serious error.
Incorrect (over-reaction): well-tolerated, rate-controlled AF in an anticoagulated patient: no life-threatening emergency.
Correct: non-critical alert; planned reassessment of rhythm control, checking adherence to anticoagulation.
tele-049.explication: Well-tolerated persistent AF with a controlled rate in a patient already anticoagulated is not life-threatening: the alert is reviewed within the usual time frame, is not critical, and warrants planned reassessment rather than immediate action. The 2024 ESC guidelines suggest considering rhythm control, especially if the AF is recent, and cardioversion requires at least 3 weeks of effective anticoagulation or a TOE. Progression to persistent AF is also a marker of disease progression to be documented. Doing nothing would miss a window to restore sinus rhythm, and stopping the anticoagulant would be a serious error: thromboembolic risk does not fall when AF becomes permanent.
tele-049.aRetenir: Well-tolerated persistent AF on anticoagulation: non-urgent, but planned reassessment of rhythm control.

tele-050.question: In an ARTESiA subgroup analysis (Lancet Neurol 2025), how did patients with prior stroke or TIA fare?
options: A higher stroke risk on aspirin, hence a greater absolute benefit
Apixaban paradoxically increased the risk of haemorrhagic stroke
The same relative and absolute benefit as the other patients
They were excluded from the trial because their stroke risk was deemed too high
commentaires: Correct: higher stroke risk on aspirin, greater absolute benefit of apixaban (subgroup analysis).
Incorrect: apixaban reduced strokes in this subgroup.
Incorrect: as their baseline risk was higher, the absolute benefit was greater.
Incorrect: they were included, as a minority, and were the subject of a subgroup analysis.
tele-050.explication: Patients with prior stroke or TIA made up a minority of ARTESiA participants but had a higher stroke risk on aspirin. Apixaban reduced strokes in this subgroup, with a greater absolute benefit than in the other patients. This illustrates the general principle of the 2024 ESC guidelines: in subclinical AF, the decision to anticoagulate depends on individual thromboembolic risk, which is highest in patients with a history of cerebrovascular events. These results nonetheless come from a subgroup analysis.
tele-050.aRetenir: Subclinical AF with prior stroke/TIA: higher risk, greater absolute benefit from DOACs.

tele-051.question: Dual-chamber pacemaker; the measured P-wave amplitude on the atrial lead has fallen from 2.5 to 0.6 mV. The AF burden counter reads 3%, whereas the clinic ECG shows AF. What is the explanation and what is the risk?
options: Far-field R-wave oversensing: AF burden overestimated by the counter
Battery depletion: the AF counter shuts down to save energy
AF undersensing: burden underestimated, falsely reassuring decision
Reliable counter: the AF was brief and the ECG happened to catch the episode
commentaires: Incorrect: far-field oversensing instead leads to overestimation of the burden.
Incorrect: nothing suggests battery depletion.
Correct: with a 0.6 mV P wave, the small AF potentials fall below the sensing threshold or into the blanking period.
Incorrect: a counter is only reliable if atrial sensing is good, which is no longer the case here.
tele-051.explication: AF electrograms are of low and highly variable amplitude. When atrial sensing is degraded, some signals fall below the sensitivity threshold and others fall into the post-ventricular blanking periods: the device no longer counts all the AF, the burden is underestimated and mode switching may be intermittent, with periods of irregular tracking. In remote monitoring, a low burden is therefore only reliable if atrial sensing is good. Atrial sensitivity should be checked and, if necessary, cautiously increased (watching for far-field sensing), and the anticoagulation decision should rely on the ECG. Far-field oversensing instead leads to overestimation.
tele-051.aRetenir: Poor atrial sensing leads to underestimation of AF burden: do not be reassured by the counter.

tele-052.question: In a patient with a cardiac implantable electronic device and subclinical AF confirmed on the EGM (with no AF on ECG), which factors favour oral anticoagulation?
options: Prior stroke or TIA
Episodes lasting more than 24 hours
High CHA2DS2-VA score
High bleeding risk
Single 20-second episode
commentaires: Correct: the absolute benefit of apixaban was greater in this ARTESiA subgroup.
Correct: episodes >24 h were associated with an increased stroke risk in ASSERT.
Correct: the benefit increases with thromboembolic risk.
Incorrect: a high bleeding risk weighs against; the 2024 ESC guidelines exclude these patients from the class IIb recommendation.
Incorrect: a single episode lasting a few seconds has no demonstrated thromboembolic significance.
tele-052.explication: The benefit of anticoagulation in subclinical AF is modest on average (NOAH-AFNET 6/ARTESiA meta-analysis: about one third fewer ischaemic strokes, more major bleeding); it grows as thromboembolic risk rises. Prior stroke/TIA (greater absolute benefit in the ARTESiA subgroup), a high CHA2DS2-VA score and long episodes (>24 h, associated with increased risk in ASSERT) point towards anticoagulation. A high bleeding risk, by contrast, weighs against it: the 2024 ESC guidelines explicitly exclude these patients from the class IIb recommendation. A single episode lasting a few seconds has no demonstrated thromboembolic significance.
tele-052.aRetenir: Subclinical AF: anticoagulation is weighed according to thromboembolic risk (prior stroke, CHA2DS2-VA, duration) and bleeding risk.

tele-053.question: An ICD patient calls the clinic: he received a single shock an hour ago and feels well, with no pain or presyncope. What do you advise?
options: Call the emergency services (15 in France) immediately for medical transport and an urgent device check
Nothing to do: the ICD did its job, mention it at the next scheduled check
Send a manual transmission for prompt review; call back if another shock or symptoms occur
Place the magnet on the device to prevent another shock, then wait for the clinic to call
commentaires: Incorrect (over-reaction): a single well-tolerated shock is not a life-threatening emergency.
Incorrect (under-reaction): every shock must be analysed; even if appropriate, it may reveal ischaemia, hypokalaemia or decompensation.
Correct: a "yellow" alert in the 2023 HRS consensus, to be handled within the working day; call the emergency services (15) for multiple shocks or symptoms.
Incorrect: the magnet suspends all protection and should only be used under medical supervision, once the diagnosis is established.
tele-053.explication: A single, well-tolerated shock in a patient who feels well is not a life-threatening emergency but must be analysed promptly: the 2023 HRS consensus classifies it as a "yellow" alert, to be handled within the working day. The key question is whether it was an appropriate shock for VT/VF, or an inappropriate one for rapid AF, sinus tachycardia, oversensing or lead noise. The transmission, manual or automatic (some systems, such as Biotronik Home Monitoring, have no patient-initiated transmission but transmit automatically after the event), provides the episode EGM. By contrast, multiple shocks (a "red" alert in the consensus), a shock followed by symptoms (pain, breathlessness, syncope) or an electrical storm call for the emergency services (15). Ignoring the shock would be a mistake: even if appropriate, it may reveal ischaemia, hypokalaemia or decompensation. Applying a magnet at home would leave the patient without any protection and without a diagnosis.
tele-053.aRetenir: Single well-tolerated shock: transmission and prompt review; multiple shocks or symptoms: emergency services (15).

tele-054.question: An ICD patient reports three shocks in one hour and feels unwell. What should be done?
options: Place a magnet on the device to suspend shocks and wait for improvement
Call the emergency services (15 in France): multiple shocks with symptoms are urgent
Send a manual transmission and wait for the remote monitoring clinic to call back
Contact the usual cardiologist for an early clinic appointment within the week
commentaires: Incorrect: the magnet should only be used under medical supervision; in an electrical storm, it removes life-saving protection.
Correct: electrical storm or repeated inappropriate shocks, both emergencies; the symptomatic patient calls the emergency services (15).
Incorrect (under-reaction): remote monitoring is not an emergency service; review may wait until the working day.
Incorrect (under-reaction): multiple shocks with feeling unwell = immediate emergency, not a deferred appointment.
tele-054.explication: Multiple shocks in quick succession, especially with symptoms, require emergency care by the SAMU (French emergency medical service): this may be an electrical storm, which is life-threatening, or repeated inappropriate shocks (lead noise, rapid AF) that must be stopped. In hospital, device interrogation guides treatment: sedation, correction of triggers, antiarrhythmic drugs, temporary deactivation of therapies if they are inappropriate. A magnet suspends therapies in most ICDs, but should only be used under medical supervision and once the diagnosis is established. The 2023 HRS consensus classifies multiple shocks as critical ("red") alerts, but remote monitoring is not an emergency service: the symptomatic patient calls the emergency services (15).
tele-054.aRetenir: Multiple shocks = call the emergency services (15), without waiting for remote monitoring.

tele-055.question: According to the 2022 ESC guidelines, how is electrical storm defined in an ICD patient?
options: At least 3 shocks, appropriate or not, over a one-month period
More than 100 PVCs per hour on a 24-hour Holter
At least 3 episodes of non-sustained VT of more than 10 beats in 24 h
At least 3 episodes of sustained VT/VF treated within 24 hours
commentaires: Incorrect: the definition refers to 24 hours and to true arrhythmias, not to inappropriate shocks.
Incorrect: frequent PVCs do not define electrical storm.
Incorrect: non-sustained VT does not meet the definition.
Correct: at least 3 separate episodes of sustained VT/VF within 24 h requiring therapy (ATP or shock).
tele-055.explication: Electrical storm is defined as at least 3 separate episodes of sustained ventricular arrhythmia within 24 hours; in an ICD patient, these are episodes requiring therapy (ATP or shock). It is an emergency associated with excess mortality, requiring hospital admission, a search for a trigger (ischaemia, potassium disturbance, HF, drugs) and often beta-blockers, amiodarone, sedation or even ablation. Frequent PVCs, non-sustained VT, shocks spread over several weeks or inappropriate shocks do not meet this definition. Remote monitoring may reveal ATP-treated episodes that the patient did not feel.
tele-055.aRetenir: Electrical storm = ≥3 treated sustained VT/VF episodes in 24 h: hospital admission.

tele-056.question: ICD remote monitoring: a single episode of monomorphic VT at 190 bpm, terminated by one ATP burst; the patient is asymptomatic and felt nothing. No other episodes. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Close the alert without calling: ATP worked and the patient felt nothing
Call the patient, look for a trigger and inform the responsible physician
Disable ATP at the next visit to avoid VT acceleration
Send the patient to the emergency department for admission, as for electrical storm
commentaires: Incorrect (under-reaction): VT is an event that may reveal ischaemia, a potassium disturbance, decompensation or non-adherence.
Correct: effective appropriate therapy, a prompt but non-life-threatening alert; look for a cause and review treatment.
Incorrect: ATP was effective and prevents shocks; disabling it would be harmful.
Incorrect (over-reaction): a single episode is not an electrical storm (≥3 in 24 h).
tele-056.explication: A single VT terminated by ATP shows that the ICD is working and is not an electrical storm. It should not, however, be closed without action: it is an arrhythmic event that may reveal ischaemia, a potassium disturbance, decompensation or non-adherence. Calling the patient and reviewing treatment (beta-blocker, antiarrhythmic drug, considering ablation if episodes recur) are indicated. ATP reduces the number of shocks and disabling it would be harmful. The level of urgency increases with recurrence, symptoms or shocks.
